Your Feed Fills Landfills

In June 2024, volunteers on the 11th floor of an office tower in Quarry Bay faced a 16-tonne mountain of donated clothes. Some still had their original tags attached and had never been worn (Knott, 2024). Yet this case is not isolated; a Hong Kong survey found that 39% of respondents had discarded clothing after wearing it just once (YouGov, 2017). But why do we buy clothes we barely wear?

Social media is part of the problem. TikTok trends like #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt introduce viewers to new products, while built-in shopping features make it easier than ever to buy them (Johnson, 2026). Research by Mahn et al. (2026) found that inspiration from fashion hauls was a major contributor to purchase intentions, especially impulsive buying. The constant pressure to follow the latest styles fuels overconsumption and increases textile waste. In Hong Kong, around 400 tonnes of textiles were sent to landfills daily in 2024 (Tsang & Ruan, 2026). However, the environmental impact extends beyond waste. Globally, the fashion industry produces 1.2 billion tonnes of CO₂ annually. If current practices persist, emissions are projected to rise by over 50% by 2030 (Johnson, 2026).

My proposed solution is an app called Rewear. It combines three features to help users reconsider unnecessary purchases and restyle clothes they already own. Although recycling can help tackle textile waste, in 2024 less than 1% of global fibre production came from recycled textiles (Tsang & Ruan, 2026), highlighting the limited role of textile recycling. The key is to prevent overconsumption.

Digital Wardrobe

Users upload photos of their clothing and create different combinations directly in the app, allowing them to recreate trending looks using existing clothes. A Hong Kong survey by Redress (2020) found that 41% of respondents owned unworn clothes because they “forgot they have it”. By helping users rediscover and restyle their clothes, the app could reduce unnecessary purchases. Jiang and Macintyre (2025) also suggest that wardrobe-management apps can encourage more sustainable clothing habits.

“Save now, decide later” wishlist

Instead of buying an item immediately, users could save it to the app. After 24 hours, they would receive a notification asking whether they still want or need it. This pause could encourage more thoughtful purchasing decisions, particularly since 46% of respondents in the same survey identified impulse-driven shopping as a reason for owning unworn clothes (Redress, 2020).

Social Platform

Users could share the outfits they created from clothes they already own, using the hashtag #OutfitRepeater. This aims to make rewearing clothes just as exciting and socially visible as showing off new purchases. Instead of going against social media culture,  Rewear uses it to encourage more sustainable behaviour.

Before expanding across Hong Kong, Rewear could be implemented through a pilot scheme at HKU, targeting young consumers who regularly engage with social media. Its effectiveness could be evaluated by tracking how often students recreated outfits without buying anything new, how many saved items were abandoned after 24 hours, and whether their self-reported impulse purchases decreased. However, photographing an entire wardrobe could be time-consuming, potentially discouraging users from engaging with the app. Instead, students could start by uploading only their most frequently worn clothes and gradually add more.

Rewear could benefit consumers by reducing unnecessary spending and helping them make better use of the clothes they already own. However, the biggest potential benefit would be environmental. According to WRAP (2012), extending the active life of clothing by nine months could reduce its carbon, water, and waste footprints by around 20–30%. By encouraging people to wear their clothes longer, Rewear could help reduce demand for new clothing and the waste its production creates. As Professor Christina Wong emphasises, tackling fashion waste requires preventing it at earlier stages rather than only managing it after disposal (Tsang & Ruan, 2026). If adopted by younger consumers, it could also encourage more sustainable consumption in the long term.

You can start right now. Although Rewear is still a proposed app, the next time you see a trending outfit on TikTok, save it instead of buying it immediately, check your wardrobe for similar pieces, and wait 24 hours before deciding whether you really need it.

The 16-tonne mountain of clothes in Quarry Bay shows what can happen when clothing is bought but barely worn. Rather than only dealing with the waste left behind, Rewear aims to tackle the problem at its source: excessive consumption. Technology has made discovering new clothes easier than ever, so why not use it to rediscover what we already own?
